tagline.text: The learned, merry prioress of the Petit-Picpus, the only cheerful woman in the convent.
The prioress who asks the gardener to break the law and bury a saint under the altar.
The prioress who admitted Fauchelevent's 'brother' as gardener and his little girl as a charity pupil.

description.text: Prioress of the Petit-Picpus from 1819 to 1825, re-elected, a short, thick woman of about sixty who sings 'like a cracked pot'. She comes of the family of a nun who wrote lives of the Benedictine saints, and is crammed with Latin, Greek, Hebrew and history, more Benedictine monk than Benedictine nun. Because she is the only merry one in the house, she is adored.

Fauchelevent finds her, for once, grave and agitated. He seizes the moment to ask leave for his 'brother', an excellent gardener, to come and help him, with a little granddaughter to be reared in the house. She does not answer. She asks only whether he can find a stout iron bar by evening, and goes off to the chapter.

Her talk runs from Dom Mabillon's count of Saint Bernard's letters to the miracles a holy tomb may work, with Fauchelevent agreeing to everything. Mother Crucifixion has died asking to lie in the vault under the chapel altar in the coffin she slept in for twenty years. The law forbids it, the chapter has agreed to it, and the gardener is to raise the slab that night and keep his mouth shut. Fauchelevent promises to fill the empty official coffin with earth. She is grateful, and tells him to bring his brother and the child the day after the burial.

She questions the new gardener herself, and Fauchelevent answers for him: Ultime Fauchelevent, from Picquigny, fifty years old, the child's grandfather. She judges that the little girl 'will grow up ugly', which reassures her about a future nun, and admits her as a charity pupil. She orders a second bell for the second gardener.
Years later Valjean tells her that his brother's death has left him a small inheritance, so he can pay for Cosette's schooling and take her away. She lets them go.

moments.text: Heard Fauchelevent ask a place for his 'brother' and asked him for an iron bar.
Ordered Mother Crucifixion buried secretly under the altar.
Admitted Ultime Fauchelevent as gardener and Cosette as a charity pupil.

tagline.text: The nun who died at the Petit-Picpus on the night Valjean dropped into its garden.
A holy nun who slept twenty years in her coffin and asked to be buried under the altar.
Buried in secret under the convent altar, while her official coffin carried someone else.

description.text: A nun of the Petit-Picpus who has just died. Her death is the convent's great event of the night, and Fauchelevent tells Valjean that her burial is why the house is in a stir.

The prioress calls her a saint. A Jansenist lady turned orthodox merely from seeing her at prayer, and the community expects her to work miracles after her death. For twenty years she slept in her own coffin. She died fully conscious, speaking to the nuns and then to the angels, and her last command was to be buried in that coffin in the vault under the chapel altar, not in profane earth. The law forbids burial in convents, so the chapter has decided to do it in secret.

Her death leaves two coffins: her own, which will go under the altar, and the empty one the authorities will send for her, which must go to the Vaugirard cemetery with something in it. Valjean proposes to be that something.
She lies under the altar as she wished. Hugo calls the burial a venial offence, one of the faults that resemble a duty: the convent dodged Caesar and satisfied God, and nobody knew.

moments.text: Her last wish, burial under the altar, is granted by the chapter.
Her empty official coffin carries Jean Valjean to the cemetery.
Lies secretly in the chapel vault.

tagline.text: The drunken old gravedigger of Vaugirard, Fauchelevent's drinking friend.
The gravedigger Fauchelevent was counting on, who turns out to be dead.

description.text: Gravedigger at the old Vaugirard cemetery, where the nuns of the Petit-Picpus have the privilege of being buried at nightfall. Fauchelevent calls him a friend.

The whole plan rests on him. He is a drunkard of the old school, says Fauchelevent: 'The gravedigger puts the corpses in the grave, and I put the gravedigger in my pocket.' Fauchelevent will take him off for a drink while the coffin waits, and come back to dig Valjean out.

At the cemetery gate a stranger tells Fauchelevent that Father Mestienne is dead. Fauchelevent had expected anything but that a gravedigger could die. It also turns out that when they drank together, Mestienne was the one who paid.

moments.text: Named as the drunk Fauchelevent will lure away from the grave.
Reported dead, replaced by Gribier.

tagline.text: The new gravedigger at Vaugirard: sober, educated, and in the way.
The gravedigger whose stolen card got Valjean out of his grave.

description.text: Father Mestienne's successor: 'After Napoleon, Louis XVIII. After Mestienne, Gribier.' Tall, thin, livid and funereal, with the air of a failed doctor. He has been a student and passed his fourth examination; his father meant him for literature, and he still earns money as a public writer. He has seven small children to feed, so he cannot drink. Fauchelevent's offer of a glass gets nowhere.

He starts shovelling earth onto the coffin. Fauchelevent sees the corner of the gravedigger's card sticking out of his pocket, slips it out, and points out that the gates will close: without his card Gribier will have to pay a fifteen-franc fine. Gribier runs home to look for it and leaves the old gardener alone with the grave. Fauchelevent later brings his tools back to his garret.
Gribier thinks only that Fauchelevent spared him the fine. He never knows what was in the coffin.

moments.text: Introduced himself at the gate: Mestienne is dead.
Lost his card to Fauchelevent and ran home to fetch it.

name: The old woman of the Gorbeau house

aliases.name: the principal lodger
aliases.note: her title in the house; in fact she is the portress

tagline.text: The old 'principal lodger' who keeps house for Valjean and Cosette in the Gorbeau hovel.
A deaf, envious, prying old woman who has seen Valjean's thousand-franc note.
The portress who told Javert everything and warned him when Valjean made ready to leave.
Dead; another old woman just like her has taken her place.

description.text: The only other person living in the Gorbeau house. She is called the 'principal lodger' but really acts as portress. She let Valjean the room on Christmas eve, believing he was a gentleman ruined by Spanish bonds, coming to live there with his little daughter. He paid six months in advance. She furnished the room and lit the stove for their arrival, and she does their cooking and marketing.

A cross-looking creature, with the inquisitiveness of the envious, a little deaf and so talkative. Through a crack in the door she watches Valjean unpick the lining of his coat and take out a thousand-franc note. When he asks her to change it, saying it is his quarterly income, she wonders where he could have got it, and tells the neighbourhood. Later she finds more papers sewn into the coat, and in its pockets a wig, a needle-case and other strange things.
Valjean hears a heavy step on the stairs at night and blows out his candle. Next morning she looks at him with her 'little polecat eyes' and says it was a new lodger.

Javert easily got her talking. She confirmed the story of the coat lined with money, since she had seen and handled the note, and Javert took a room in the house. When she heard a coin fall in Valjean's room, she guessed he was leaving and hurried to tell Javert.

moments.text: Spied Valjean taking a thousand-franc note from his coat lining.
Told Valjean the step on the stairs was a new lodger.
Warned Javert that Valjean meant to leave.

aliases.name: Madame Burgon
aliases.note: her real name; Courfeyrac, who respects nothing, renamed her

tagline.text: The old woman who keeps the Gorbeau house and sweeps its stairs.
The old portress of the Gorbeau house, astounded to see Marius go out in his new coat three days running.
The portress whose evening out washing dishes leaves the Gorbeau house empty.
The portress who tells the singing gamin where his whole family has been taken.

description.text: The portress and housekeeper of the Gorbeau house on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, a grumbling old woman who does what little cleaning the tenants get.

The 'principal tenant', portress and housekeeper of the Gorbeau house, the old woman who replaced Valjean's prying landlady. Her life has nothing remarkable in it but three parakeets, one after another. For three francs a month she sweeps Marius's room and brings his hot water, egg and roll. When he goes out in his new coat on three days in a row, she cannot get over it.
She is sweeping the doorstep and talking to herself when Marius goes out. Once a pair of old boots went missing from his room and she triumphed, because he never locks his door.

Every evening she goes out to wash dishes in town, and she locks the house when she leaves. Jondrette is counting on that: at six o'clock the neighbour will be at dinner and Mother Bougon out, and there will be no one to hear.

The night after the ambush a ragged gamin kicks at the locked door, asking to see 'his ancestors'. She tells him his father is at La Force, his mother at Saint-Lazare and his sisters at the Madelonettes. He says 'Ah!', pirouettes, and goes off singing.

moments.text: Thunderstruck by Marius's new coat, three days running.
Locked up the house and went out as the trap was being set.
Told Gavroche that his whole family was in prison.

aliases.name: Fabantou
aliases.note: the 'dramatic artist' who signed the letter to the gentleman of Saint-Jacques

aliases.name: Monsieur Jondrette
aliases.note: his wife's slip, explained away as an artistic sobriquet

tagline.text: The destitute lodger of the Gorbeau garret, father of a gamin he never thinks of.
Marius's neighbour, about to be put out for twenty francs of rent.
A begging-letter writer who signs a different name for every patron.
A small, grey-bearded man in a woman's chemise who curses the rich and writes for their money.
'Fabantou, dramatic artist', putting on a show of misery for M. Leblanc.
A man who says he knows his benefactor from eight years ago and is laying a trap for him.
The host of a trap who drops his mask and asks his prisoner: 'Do you know me?'

description.text: He lives with his wife and two grown daughters in one attic room of the Gorbeau house, the poorest household in a house full of poor people. When he took the room he gave his name as Jondrette, and told the portress that anyone asking for a Pole, an Italian or perhaps a Spaniard meant him. The boy Gavroche is his son. He does not think of him, the mother does not love him, and when the boy visits he finds a cold hearth and cold hearts.
In 1831 Marius hears that the Jondrettes, his neighbours across the partition, are to be turned out for twenty francs of rent. He pays it secretly, with five francs more for them.

His elder daughter brings Marius a begging letter in the same hand as the four letters Marius found on the boulevard: the same coarse paper, the same tobacco smell, the same spelling mistakes. Those letters were signed Don Alvarès, a Spanish captain; Mistress Balizard, a mother of six; Genflot, a man of letters; and P. Fabantou, a dramatic artist. One writer is behind all four.

Through the hole in the wall Marius sees him: about sixty, small, thin and livid, with a cunning, cruel and uneasy look and a long grey beard, in a woman's chemise over muddy trousers. There is no bread in the garret, but there is tobacco. He smokes and writes, raging that even the dead are unequal and that he could eat the whole world. His huge wife calls him her 'little friend'.

When word comes that the gentleman from Saint-Jacques is on his way, he stages his misery in minutes. He puts out the fire, kicks the seat out of the chair, has the younger girl put her fist through a windowpane (she cuts her hand), and sends his wife to bed. While they wait he rails against rich men who bring old clothes and bread when what the poor want is money.

Before M. Leblanc and his daughter he plays Fabantou: a pupil of Talma, once favoured by fortune and now without bread or fire, his wife ill and his child wounded. He pinches the girl's cut hand to make her cry out. He claims to owe sixty francs of rent by the next day, which Marius knows is a lie. Leblanc leaves five francs and his greatcoat and promises to come back at six with the money. All the while Jondrette studies him strangely and whispers to his wife to take a good look at the man.

Alone with his wife he exults: eight years have passed, but he recognises the man. He whispers something about the young lady that puts his wife into a monstrous rage. His 'fortune is made'. At six the house will be empty; the 'Croesus' will pay, and if he does not, 'we'll fix him'. He orders a charcoal brazier and goes out to see 'some people'.

Marius follows him through the snow in Leblanc's greatcoat. He visits a hovel in the Rue Gracieuse, buys a large cold chisel at an ironmonger's, and climbs over a low wall where Marius has heard two men plotting with Patron-Minette. That evening he tells his family that all is going well: 'The mousetrap is open. The cats are there.'

The garret is ready: a brazier of glowing charcoal with the chisel heating in it, ropes, iron, a rope ladder. He tests a kitchen knife and sends his wife down with a lantern to admit the visitor and send away his cab.

Across the table from Leblanc, who has laid four louis down for the rent, he keeps up his patter: his poverty, his girls, the paper-box trade, thoughts of drowning himself. Meanwhile four men with blackened faces slip in behind him. He offers his one treasure, 'a picture by a master'. Leblanc says it is some tavern signboard worth three francs. Jondrette asks a thousand crowns. Then his eyes flash and he cries out: 'Do you know me?'

moments.text: Had his rent paid without knowing it by the neighbour, Marius.
Wrecked his own garret to look poorer before the benefactor came.
Played Fabantou, the ruined actor, for M. Leblanc.
Told his wife he had recognised the visitor and would 'fix him'.
Bought a cold chisel and met with accomplices.
Sprang his trap: 'Do you know me?'

aliases.name: Nicolette
aliases.note: the name M. Gillenormand gave every maid, Magnon among them

tagline.text: One of M. Gillenormand's maids, all of whom he called Nicolette.
The dismissed maid who sent M. Gillenormand two newborn boys and is paid to bring them up.
A woman watched by the police, a go-between for the underworld with ties to the Thénardiers.
The woman who swapped her own dead sons for the Thénardiers' two youngest to keep her eighty francs a month.

description.text: Every maid in M. Gillenormand's house is renamed Nicolette, and among them was 'a certain Magnon'.

Six months after being dismissed, she sent the eighty-four-year-old Gillenormand a yelling newborn boy in a basket and named him as the father. Flattered rather than angry, he denied it and had the child looked after. A year later she sent a second boy. He gave in: both went back to their mother with eighty francs a month for their keep, on condition she sent no more, and he visits them from time to time.
The Nicolette now in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire is her successor.

When Brujon's coded note about 'an affair in the Rue Plumet' leaves La Force, it passes from woman to woman to her. She is strongly suspected by the police but not yet arrested, and she has dealings with the Thénardiers that Hugo promises to explain. She gets it to Éponine, newly out of prison. The answer comes back through her: 'biscuit', nothing to be done.

Her two boys died of croup on the same day, one in the morning and one in the evening, and with them went the eighty francs a month. The Thénardiers had two sons of the same age that they did not want, so the little Thénardiers became little Magnons. Thénardier took ten francs a month of the money. The boys were well kept, since profit was attached to them, and better treated by their false mother than they had been by their real one. She played the lady and spoke no slang in front of them. After the Gorbeau arrests the police raided her house in the Rue Clocheperce and took her and her companion, Mamselle Miss. The two boys, out playing in the yard, came back to a locked and empty house, with only a scrap of paper bearing an address.
Her two 'sons' are still in the street: the Thénardiers' children, leased to her, attributed to M. Gillenormand, and left like leaves for the wind to blow about.

moments.text: Sent M. Gillenormand two babies and got eighty francs a month for them.
Passed Brujon's Rue Plumet note to Éponine.
Arrested in a raid on the Rue Clocheperce, leaving the two boys locked out.

aliases.name: Luc-Esprit Gillenormand
aliases.note: the names his godfather gave him, predicting genius

tagline.text: A hale, loud, cane-swinging bourgeois of over ninety, left over from the eighteenth century.
An old gallant who pays for two babies he swears are not his, and calls his dead daughter's husband the disgrace of the family.
A tyrant of a grandfather who bullies the small boy in his house and idolises him.
The grandfather who took Marius from his father, Colonel Pontmercy, on pain of disinheritance.
The grandfather who turned Marius out of the house over his father's title.
A proud old man secretly pining for the grandson he threw out.
The grandfather who refused Marius's marriage with an insult and watched him walk out again.
The grandfather who thought Marius dead in his drawing-room, and fainted when he opened his eyes.
The grandfather who gives Marius his Cosette and is called 'father' at last.

description.text: In 1831 he is over ninety and very much alive: he walks erect, talks loudly, eats, drinks and snores, has all thirty-two of his teeth, and wears spectacles only to read. He is the complete and rather haughty bourgeois of the eighteenth century. He claims to have given up women, not because he is too old but because he is too poor. When contradicted he raises his cane, as men did in the great century. He scolds his unmarried daughter of over fifty as if she were eight.

He owns No. 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire in the Marais and lives on its first floor among Gobelins tapestries, a Coromandel screen and a boudoir hung with straw-work made by Louis XIV's convicts. He dresses like a Directory dandy. He has had two wives, and was the kind of husband always deceived by his wives and never by his mistresses. The French Revolution, he says, was a heap of blackguards.

Born at Moulins, he still glories in a school prize given him there by the Duc de Nivernais. He adores the Bourbons, turns purple at any praise of the Republic, and tells again and again how his wit saved his head in the Terror. At ninety he hopes 'not to see ninety-three twice', which means he intends to live to a hundred.

His theory of marriage is that a philandering husband should give the purse-strings to a disagreeable wife, who will console herself by ruining him. His second wife did exactly that, and he lives on an annuity of fifteen thousand francs that will mostly die with him. He renames every servant: the valet becomes Basque, after his province, and every maid is Nicolette.

At eighty-four he was sent a newborn boy by a dismissed maid, Magnon, who said it was his. He was flattered, not angry. He denied it, paid for it, and paid again for a second boy the next year, eighty francs a month for both. He gives gladly and grandly. By his first wife he has an unmarried daughter. By his second he had a daughter who died at about thirty after marrying for love a soldier of the Republic and the Empire, made colonel at Waterloo. 'He is the disgrace of my family.'

Hugo sums him up as frivolous and great. He left the Faubourg Saint-Germain for the Marais after eighty, and keeps his door shut all day to everyone, the king included: the day is vulgar, he says, and deserves a closed shutter. He receives only after dinner at five.

A small boy lives in the house, always trembling and mute before him. The old man speaks to him only severely, sometimes with his cane raised, and calls him rascal and scoundrel, and he idolises him. The boy is his grandson.

Around 1817 he is the lion of the Baronne de T.'s ultra-Royalist salon in the Rue Férou, where Napoleon is mocked and liberals cursed. He brings his daughter and a handsome boy of seven, whom the old ladies pity as 'poor child' because his father is a 'brigand of the Loire'.

The brigand is his son-in-law, Colonel Georges Pontmercy. Gillenormand claimed the grandson when the mother died, threatening to disinherit him otherwise, and the colonel gave way. He may never see or speak to the boy, Marius, on pain of his being disowned. Gillenormand never mentions the colonel except to mock 'his Baronship'.

In 1827 a letter comes from Vernon: the colonel is ill and asks for his son. Gillenormand tells the seventeen-year-old to set out the next day. Neither of them thinks of the night coach, and Marius arrives too late. Afterwards he has the colonel's sword and uniform sold to an old-clothes dealer.

He finds the medallion Marius has started wearing, opens it hoping for a love letter, and reads instead the colonel's bequest of his barony: 'It is the slasher's handwriting.' Then the cards fall out: 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy'. Their quarrel ends with Marius shouting 'Down with the Bourbons!' The old man bows to a bust of the Duc de Berry, and tells his daughter that a baron and a bourgeois cannot stay under one roof. 'Be off!' He orders sixty pistoles sent to 'that blood-drinker' every six months and forbids his name to be spoken.

He is not what Marius thinks. He idolised the boy, boxing his ears all the while, and the house is now a black void. He expected the 'Jacobin' to come back, and years pass. He never asks about him and thinks of him all the time. 'Oh! if he only would return, what a good box on the ear I would give him!'

His daughter brings in Théodule as a substitute grandson. Gillenormand forgets him at once and paces the room, raging at students, republicans, romantics and the century, and at the absent Marius, while the lancer agrees with everything. When Théodule cries that it is 'wonderfully true', the old man wheels round and tells him: 'You are a fool.'
He is still paying Magnon's eighty francs a month. Her own sons died long ago; the boys the money now feeds are two little Thénardiers.

At ninety-one he is sinking inwardly. He keeps his dead daughter's portrait opposite his bed, says it looks like 'him' too, and forbids Marius's name to be spoken. When Basque announces 'M. Marius', joy makes him harsh: what has the young man come for? Permission to marry, a girl without a dowry. 'Never!' But the word 'Father' melts him. He gives Marius a hundred louis for a hat and listens to the whole story. At 'Rue Plumet' he remembers Théodule's tale of a girl behind a railing there, and gives the old man's advice: 'make her your mistress.' Marius answers that five years ago he insulted his father and today he has insulted his wife, and leaves. The old man shouts 'Marius!' from the window four times, then falls back in his chair.
On the night of 6 June a police agent hammers at his door: his 'son' has been brought back dead from the barricade. The servants and his daughter are woken. He is left to sleep.

Woken by the light under his door, he stands on the threshold in his white dressing-gown like a phantom and sees Marius bleeding on a mattress. He decides the boy is dead and rages: Marius got himself killed on the barricades to spite him, when his room was ready and his portrait hung by the bed, and he had only to come back and say 'It is I'. He talks to the doctor with terrible calm, then bends over the body muttering 'clubbist' and 'Septembrist'. Marius opens his eyes. 'My child! My well-beloved son!' cries the old man, and falls fainting.

Through months of fever he moves his armchair to the bedside, insists on the finest linen for lint, and asks the doctor the same questions over and over. The day Marius is out of danger he dances a gavotte and sings a bawdy song. Basque sees him praying, he who never believed in God. He calls Marius 'M. le Baron' and shouts 'Long live the Republic!', becoming, in Hugo's phrase, the grandson of his grandson. Marius, still remembering his father's wrongs, stays cold.

When Marius announces with a terrible look that he wishes to marry, the old man says 'Agreed' and bursts out laughing. He has made inquiries: the girl's old gentleman comes to ask after Marius every day, she lives at No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé, and the lancer story was false. He confesses he hoped that giving Marius Cosette would make Marius love him a little. They weep in each other's arms, and Marius calls him 'father'. Then he blunders into abusing the men of '93 and has to rush out and shout at Basque about André Chénier.

He greets Cosette with 'Adorable!', asks for her hand on behalf of Baron Marius Pontmercy, and calls her guardian 'Monsieur Tranchelevent'. When he laments that his annuity will leave the young couple poor, Fauchelevent answers that Mademoiselle Euphrasie Fauchelevent has six hundred thousand francs. 'This is a fine book,' says Gillenormand of the package.

He showers Cosette with lace, moiré and old jewels from his lacquered chests, preaches the philosophy of the superfluous, and laments that the century has forgotten how to marry. He gives the couple his own room, hung with buttercup satin, and turns his library into Marius's study.

He gives the bride away in the elegance of the Barras era, taking the place of her father, whose arm is in a sling. When M. Fauchelevent's chair stays empty at the banquet, he puts Marius in it and toasts love: be Daphnis and Chloe now and Philemon and Baucis later.
He is ninety-six and wants no new attachments. When the household wonders at M. Fauchelevent's evening visits to the lower room, he settles the matter: 'He's an original.'

moments.text: Agreed to pay for Magnon's two babies while denying they were his.
Found the colonel's note, and turned Marius out of the house.
Told Théodule, 'You are a fool.'
Told Marius to make Cosette his mistress, and lost him again.
Fainted for joy when the 'dead' Marius opened his eyes.
Consented to the marriage; Marius called him 'father'.
Gave Cosette away and toasted love at the wedding feast.

aliases.name: Mademoiselle Gillenormand the elder
aliases.note: no one outside the family knows her first name

tagline.text: M. Gillenormand's unmarried elder daughter, past fifty and scolded like a child.
A prude and bigot who keeps her father's house and dotes on a lancer grand-nephew.
The aunt who sends Théodule to spy on Marius's supposed love affair.
The aunt whose money Marius keeps sending back.
The aunt trying to slip Théodule into Marius's place.
An old maid won over to the marriage by six hundred thousand francs.

description.text: Daughter of M. Gillenormand's first wife, she never married. Her younger half-sister married a soldier of the Empire and died.

The two sisters were born ten years apart and were nothing alike. The younger dreamed of a hero; the elder dreamed of a rich contractor and of being 'Madame la Préfète'. One had wings like an angel, Hugo says, the other like a goose. She is now an antique virtue and an incombustible prude with a sharp nose and a dull mind, who cherishes the frightful memory of a man once glimpsing her garter. Yet she lets her grand-nephew Théodule, an officer of Lancers, kiss her. She is devout, never malicious, and gives off the stupor of a life finished without ever having begun. She keeps house for her father, as the Bishop's sister kept house for him.
She is rich in her own right from her mother's side, and her sister's son, Marius, is her natural heir. It is she who takes him to mass at Saint-Sulpice.

Marius keeps disappearing for days. She decides there is a love affair, and pays Théodule ten louis to follow him on the diligence and report. The 'lass' Théodule finds is a grave at Vernon, and he writes her nothing.

She puts on her spectacles to read the colonel's note in Marius's medallion with her father, and both feel chilled as by a death's-head. After Marius is thrown out, her father orders her to send him sixty pistoles every six months, and speaks to her coldly for three months.
She finds out where Marius lives and sends him sixty pistoles. He sends them back, and goes on returning every sum she sends.
She thinks too little to love much. She cares more for her cat or her parakeet than for the missing nephew.
Having used Théodule to spy on Marius, she now plans to have him replace Marius in the old man's affections, and whispers to him to approve of everything his great-uncle says. It does not work.
She ventures to ask whether her father is still angry with poor Marius, and is told never to mention him. When Marius does come, she is called in to say good day and sent out again.
On the night Marius is carried in, she wrings her hands, worries that everything will be covered with blood, and stops just short of 'I told you so', then withdraws to tell her beads.

She takes M. Fauchelevent's mouldy-looking package for a book, and watches this burst of light into her failed life with stupefied innocence. When the package turns out to hold five hundred and eighty-four thousand francs, she murmurs the sum over and over.

Piqued that her father never consulted her about the marriage, she had kept the question of her own inheritance open. But one owes consideration to six hundred thousand francs, so she decides to leave her fortune to the young couple, who do not need it.

moments.text: Paid Théodule to shadow Marius to Vernon.
Sent Marius money, which he returned.
Presented Théodule as a substitute grandson.
Resolved to leave her fortune to Marius and Cosette.

tagline.text: Mademoiselle Gillenormand's favourite, a grand-nephew in the Lancers.
The lancer paid to spy on Marius, who finds him weeping on his father's grave.
The would-be substitute grandson who agrees with everything and is called a fool.
The handsome lancer who rides past Cosette's gate every day.
Captain now, a wedding guest who recognises no one.

description.text: A grand-nephew and officer of Lancers, the one man the prudish Mademoiselle Gillenormand allows to kiss her.

For ten louis from his aunt he takes the Vernon diligence behind Marius to find out who the 'lass' is. He watches Marius buy flowers and go behind the church, and finds him sobbing on a grave marked 'Colonel Baron Pontmercy'.
Abashed before the grave, he retreats with something like a military salute, and decides not to write to his aunt.

Garrisoned in Paris, he calls in plain clothes, calculating that the old druid has not sunk all his money in an annuity. Told by his aunt to approve of everything, he stammers 'Good day, uncle' and spends the visit chiming in with 'That is true' and 'You are right, uncle' while M. Gillenormand rails at the century. At last he ventures that the doctrine is 'wonderfully true', and the old man calls him a fool.
He is now stationed at the barracks near the Rue Plumet. Every day he rides past Cosette's gate, handsome and well aware of it, and for a while she watches for him.
Once she has read Marius's notebook, the same lancer passing at the same hour looks hideous to her.

He has told his great-uncle about a girl he has been courting behind a railing in the Rue Plumet, which leads the old man to his fatal advice to Marius. As a substitute grandson he has failed: a vulgar chatterbox in a tricoloured cockade, who only makes the old man miss Marius more.

Now a captain, he comes from Chartres for his cousin's wedding. Cosette does not recognise him, and he remembers her no better than any other woman, so the grandfather congratulates himself on never having believed the lancer's story.

moments.text: Followed Marius to Vernon and found him at his father's grave.
Agreed with his great-uncle once too often: 'You are a fool.'
Caught Cosette's eye from the street outside her gate.
Attended Marius's wedding without recognising the bride.

aliases.name: the brigand of the Loire
aliases.note: what the Royalists called Napoleon's disbanded officers

aliases.name: Colonel Baron Pontmercy
aliases.note: the title Napoleon gave him at Waterloo, which the Restoration refuses to recognise

tagline.text: A wounded cuirassier officer, pulled from under the dead at Waterloo by a man who is robbing him.
Colonel Georges Pontmercy, hero of the Empire, growing flowers at Vernon, forbidden to see his son Marius.
The colonel who died calling for the son who came too late, leaving him his title and a debt to a sergeant.
The father Marius discovers only after his death, and comes to worship.

description.text: On the night after Waterloo a prowler stripping the dead in the hollow road of Ohain pulls an officer out from under a heap of bodies. He is a cuirassier of high rank with a big gold epaulette, his face laid open by a sword-cut. The prowler takes his cross of the Legion of Honour, his watch and his purse before the officer opens his eyes. The officer thanks him, asks who won, and tells him to take his watch and purse; the man says there is nothing there. 'You have saved my life. Who are you?' A sergeant, says the man, named Thénardier. 'I shall not forget that name, and do you remember mine. My name is Pontmercy.'

Around 1817 he lives at Vernon in the smallest house he could find, a man of about fifty in sabots and a leather cap, with a great scar from forehead to cheek, growing tulips and dahlias the whole town admires. He is shy, drinks milk, and a child can make him give way. His name runs through twenty years of bulletins, from the army of the Rhine to Austerlitz, Eylau, Moscow and Elba. At Waterloo he captured a standard and threw it at the Emperor's feet, covered in blood, and Napoleon made him a colonel and a baron on the spot; an hour later he fell into the sunken road. The Restoration put him on half-pay under surveillance and refuses his titles. He signs himself 'Colonel Baron Pontmercy' anyway, and sends back unopened any letter addressed to 'Commandant'.

Between two wars he married M. Gillenormand's younger daughter, who died in 1815 leaving a little boy. The grandfather claimed the child on pain of disinheritance, and the colonel gave way for the boy's sake and gave his love to his flowers. He may never see or speak to his son. Every two or three months he slips into Paris like a criminal breaking his ban and stands behind a pillar at Saint-Sulpice to watch Marius at mass, weeping. The churchwarden there, M. Mabeuf, is the brother of his curé at Vernon.

In 1827 brain fever takes him. He writes to ask for his son. On the evening Marius arrives he rises from his bed in delirium crying 'My son is not coming! I shall go to meet him!', falls, and dies, with a tear still on his cheek. Marius feels nothing. The colonel leaves a note: the Emperor made him a baron at Waterloo; since the Restoration disputes the title, his son is to take it and be worthy of it. At Waterloo a sergeant named Thénardier saved his life, a man who now keeps an inn near Paris, at Chelles or Montfermeil; if his son meets him, he is to do him all the good he can. His sword and uniform are sold; the neighbours pillage his garden.

Old Mabeuf tells Marius why he prizes his chair at Saint-Sulpice: from there he watched, for ten years, a poor father come secretly to gaze at the son he was forbidden to see. Marius learns that the father was Colonel Pontmercy.

Marius reads the history of the Republic and the Empire, and the father he neglected becomes a hero to him, and Napoleon with him. He has cards printed, 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', wears the colonel's note round his neck, and searches Montfermeil for the sergeant. The inn has failed and Thénardier has vanished.

When the grandfather sneers, Marius gives his father's epitaph: a humble, heroic man who served the Republic and France for twenty-five years, took two flags and twenty wounds, and died forgotten, his one mistake to have loved two ingrates too well, his country and his son. The note is lost on the attic stairs, and Marius believes his grandfather burned it.

The note's command catches up with Marius in the Gorbeau garret. The man about to torture a prisoner names himself Thénardier of Montfermeil, the sergeant of Waterloo, and the painted sign shows one soldier carrying another out of battle. Marius cannot bring himself to fire on the man his father told him to help.
Outside the barricade, Marius feels that civil war would desecrate his father's sword. Then he reasons that there is only just and unjust war, and that the monarchy itself is a foreigner.

Marius at last pays the debt his father left him, to the man who robbed him on the battlefield, thinking he is paying for a rescue. 'Waterloo protects you,' he tells Thénardier, and Thénardier corrects him: it was a general he saved.

moments.text: Pulled alive from the hollow road of Ohain and robbed by Thénardier, whom he thanked.
Watched his son in secret at Saint-Sulpice for ten years.
Died at Vernon calling for Marius, leaving him his barony and a debt to Thénardier.
His grave at Vernon is where Marius goes when he 'sleeps out'.

tagline.text: M. Gillenormand's maid, whoever she happens to be: he calls them all Nicolette.
The maid who lost the colonel's note on the dark attic stairs.
The maid who dressed Cosette for her wedding.

description.text: Every maid who enters M. Gillenormand's service is renamed Nicolette. A haughty cook called Olympie asked thirty francs a month; he offered fifty on condition she be called Nicolette.
The present Nicolette took over from Magnon, and serves the old man in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire with Basque and the porter.

Ordered to carry away Marius's 'duds', the coat, the black ribbon and the medallion, she drops the case on the dark attic stairs. It is never found. Marius believes his grandfather burned his father's last words.
On the night Marius is brought home, Basque wakes her and she wakes the aunt. She opens the linen presses, and later tears and rolls bandages for the doctor.
With Toussaint she dresses Cosette for the wedding in white taffeta, Binche lace and orange blossom.
She sweeps the spiders out of the lower room where M. Fauchelevent insists on being received. Toussaint cannot get on with her and leaves.
Cosette sends her to ask why M. Jean has not come. He tells her he is not ill, only busy, and that it has been two days since he was there; she does not pass that on.

moments.text: Lost the medallion with the colonel's note on the stairs.
Dressed the bride.
Carried Cosette's message to M. Jean and his evasions back.

tagline.text: M. Gillenormand's stout, short-winded valet, named after his province.
The old valet who announces 'M. Marius' after four years.
The valet who ushers M. Fauchelevent in, and then shows him to the lower room.

description.text: M. Gillenormand names his menservants after their province. His latest valet, a stout, short-winded fellow of fifty-five from Bayonne, became Basque.

These days the old man no longer bangs the landing with his cane when Basque is slow at the door. One evening Basque comes in to announce a young man who says he is M. Marius. When Marius leaves, Basque and Nicolette hold their master back at the window as he shouts after him.
The porter wakes him on the night of 6 June, and he runs for a doctor while Marius bleeds on the sofa.
He sees his master kneeling on a chair in prayer, the old man who never believed in God.
Collared in the anteroom by a purple-faced M. Gillenormand bellowing that 'those ruffians' assassinated André Chénier, he answers 'Yes, sir' in alarm.
At the wedding banquet he brings word that M. Fauchelevent's injured hand pains him, that he begs to be excused and has gone.
He waits in the courtyard for M. Fauchelevent at the appointed hour and shows him into the damp ground-floor room he has asked for, setting a candle on the chimneypiece.
The fire in the lower room stops being lit and the armchairs disappear. When Cosette asks why, M. Jean says he told Basque to remove them himself.
He brings Marius a coarse, tobacco-scented letter and says the writer is waiting in the antechamber.

moments.text: Announced M. Marius to his grandfather.
Ran for the doctor the night Marius was brought home.
Showed in a stranger in green spectacles.

tagline.text: The small mountain see in the south of France where M. Myriel is bishop.
The town that turned away a ragged ex-convict from every door but one.
Where the Bishop gave Jean Valjean his silver and told him he had bought his soul for God.

description.text: A cathedral town in the Alps of Provence, seat of the bishop M. Myriel since 1806. Its diocese is nearly all mountain and nearly roadless, with thirty-two curacies and hundreds of chapels, and the Bishop visits them on foot, by cart or on a donkey.
Three days after arriving, the Bishop gives his spacious palace to the cramped hospital next door and moves into the hospital's little house. The town calls him Monseigneur Bienvenu.

Digne shuns the old member of the Convention who lives alone outside the town as a near-regicide; only its bishop visits him, and kneels for his blessing. After nine years the town loves its bishop, even while it adores the emperor he snubbed.

In October 1815 a traveller in rags with a knapsack and a cudgel walks into Digne at dusk. Both inns refuse him, the prison will not take him, a family drives him from its door, and even a dog's kennel throws him out. An old woman points him to the little house beside the Bishop's palace.

He leaves Digne the next morning with the Bishop's silver and candlesticks, as if fleeing. On the plain outside the town he steals forty sous from a little Savoyard, searches for the boy in vain, and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. That night he is seen kneeling at the Bishop's door.
Early in 1820 the papers announce the death of Monseigneur Bienvenu, Bishop of Digne, blind in his last years and tended by his sister.

moments.text: The Bishop gave his palace to the hospital.
Every door in town shut on Jean Valjean.
The Bishop gave Valjean the candlesticks and 'bought his soul' for God.
The Bishop of Digne died.

tagline.text: The naval prison where Jean Valjean spent nineteen years.
The galleys whose old convicts and guards swear they know Jean Valjean.
Where Jean Valjean is sent back for life, as convict number 9,430.
The prison Valjean escaped by falling into its harbour.

description.text: The traveller turned away all over Digne tells the Bishop's household plainly what he is: Jean Valjean, nineteen years in the galleys, freed four days ago, carrying a yellow passport that marks him as very dangerous wherever he shows it.
He was sent there in 1796 for breaking a baker's window and stealing a loaf for his sister's starving children, and became number 24,601. Attempts to escape stretched five years to nineteen.

The galleys made a hard, silent, hating man of him. He was worth four men at the capstan and was nicknamed Jean the Jackscrew after holding up a balcony of the Toulon town hall on his shoulders. He learned to climb the inside angle of two walls with only his back, elbows and heels.

Javert was once a guard at Toulon. So the old convicts Brevet, Chenildieu and Cochepaille, and Javert himself, can all swear before the Arras court that the apple-thief Champmathieu is the Jean Valjean they knew there.
In July 1823 the recaptured Jean Valjean is tried for robbing Little Gervais, condemned to death and reprieved to hard labour for life, and taken back to Toulon. He is now number 9,430.

In late October 1823 the warship Orion puts into Toulon harbour for repairs, and convicts are working aboard when a sailor is left hanging from a yard. The Toulon paper reports that convict 9,430, Jean Valjean, drowned saving him.
He threw himself into the harbour unchained, swam underwater to a moored boat, hid there until night, and reached the shore near Cape Brun. From there he made his way north to Paris.
Hugo's history of slang goes down to the cellar of the old Châtelet, where men bound for Toulon were chained standing in the mud, and where nearly all the galley songs were born.

moments.text: Jean Valjean became prisoner 24,601 in 1796.
Valjean was sent back for life as number 9,430.
A convict fell from the Orion's rigging into the harbour and was reported drowned.

tagline.text: The northern town where Fantine was born.
A town of black-glass trinket makers, made rich by a stranger who arrived in 1815.
The prosperous town whose factory owner, M. Madeleine, is now its mayor.
The town where Jean Valjean has lived for eight years as M. Madeleine.
A town fallen back into poverty since its mayor was arrested.

description.text: Fantine's birthplace, in the north of France. She had no known parents and no family name, and left it as a child.
Left with no money and a child to hide, Fantine thinks of going back to her native town, where someone might know her and give her work, so long as no one learns about Cosette.

The town has always lived by imitating English jet and German black glass, a trade held back by the cost of its raw material. At the end of 1815 a stranger in workman's clothes arrived on a December evening, ran into a burning town hall to save two children, and was never asked for his passport. He changed the materials and the method, cut the costs, raised the wages, and made the whole town prosperous. Fantine finds it transformed.
Father Madeleine's factory takes anyone willing to be honest, men and women apart. His money builds schools, a hospital wing and a fund for old workmen. In 1820 he is made mayor.
The town has one sceptic, the police inspector Javert, who watches the mayor.

It is a small town, and in small towns gossip rules. A pious widow pays for a trip to Montfermeil to find out about Fantine's letters, and spreads the news of her child. Fantine is dismissed from the factory in the mayor's name and told to leave the district.
She cannot leave for her debts. In the town where she was born she sells her hair, then her two front teeth, and finally herself.
The mayor's secret is now told: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean, who settled here after Digne to hide his name and to do good. The candlesticks on his mantel are the Bishop's.
When the mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer stands up in court at Arras and declares himself Jean Valjean, the town loses him.
Javert arrests him beside Fantine's deathbed. He breaks out of the town jail, slips back into his house one last time, and leaves for Paris.

Without him the town's prosperity collapses. Rival manufacturers set up, methods and products are debased, workshops close, wages fall, bankruptcy follows, and the poor are left with nothing. Within four years the cost of collecting the district's taxes has doubled.
Cosette's six hundred thousand francs are what M. Madeleine earned at Montreuil-sur-Mer, withdrawn from Laffitte's bank in time and buried for ten years in the forest of Montfermeil.

moments.text: A stranger saved two children from the burning town hall on the night he arrived.
M. Madeleine became mayor.
Fantine was dismissed from the factory.
The town's industry collapsed after the mayor's arrest.

name: The Sergeant of Waterloo (the Montfermeil inn)

tagline.text: A cook-shop at Montfermeil, near Paris, kept by the Thénardiers, under a sign of one soldier carrying another.
The inn where Cosette is a drudge and the Thénardiers' daughters are queens.
The inn from which a stranger took Cosette away on Christmas morning, 1823.
A failed and shuttered inn; its landlord has vanished.
Its old signboard turns up in a Paris garret, offered as 'a picture by a master'.

description.text: In the spring of 1818 Fantine stops at a low cook-shop in Montfermeil because two little girls are swinging, laughing, in the loop of a chain under a wrecked cart outside it. The sign above the door is a daub of a man carrying a general on his back through smoke and blood, lettered 'Au Sargent de Waterloo'. She asks the landlady to keep her child. A man's voice from inside sets the terms: seven francs a month, fifty-seven francs in advance, and the child's fine clothes into the bargain.

The landlord, Thénardier, says he was a sergeant in the 1815 campaign and painted the sign himself to record a feat of arms. Hugo pointedly reserves judgement on how much of that is true. The house is failing, and Fantine's money goes straight to pay one of its notes.

The Thénardiers pawn Cosette's clothes, dress her in rags and feed her under the table with the dog and cat, while they keep raising the price they charge her mother. Before she is five she is sweeping, carrying and running errands. The village calls her the Lark.

By 1823 the inn is going badly. Thénardier tells customers that at Waterloo he carried a gravely wounded general out of the grapeshot, which is how the house got its sign and its name. Hugo says he in fact followed the armies as a marauding sutler.

On Christmas eve 1823 the inn is full of carters and pedlars drinking, and a pedlar's horse needs water. Across the street a toy stall shows a magnificent doll, and Cosette is sent out into the dark to fetch water from the spring.
A shabby stranger who came in with her and the bucket is charged double. He buys Cosette the doll from the stall and leaves a gold louis in her wooden shoe.
Before dawn he pays a padded bill and fifteen hundred francs to take Cosette away, and the two walk out of Montfermeil on the road to Livry.
Colonel Pontmercy's note says the sergeant who saved him now keeps a little inn near Paris, at Chelles or Montfermeil.
Marius goes to Montfermeil to find it. The inn has failed and closed, and no one knows where Thénardier has gone.
The daub Jondrette tried to sell M. Leblanc for a thousand crowns is the old sign: a battle, smoke, one man carrying another. Marius sees in it his father's rescue.

moments.text: Fantine left Cosette with the Thénardiers here.
A stranger bought Cosette the doll from the stall across the street.
Cosette left the inn for good with the stranger.
Marius found the inn closed and its landlord gone.

aliases.name: Mont-Saint-Jean
aliases.note: the plateau at the heart of the battle

aliases.name: the hollow road of Ohain
aliases.note: the sunken road that swallowed the cuirassiers

tagline.text: The Belgian battlefield of 18 June 1815, walked by the narrator in 1861.
Where Napoleon's cuirassiers rode into a hidden sunken road and filled it with their bodies.
The battle where the Guard died and the Empire ended.
A field of the dead, robbed by night, where a prowler pulled an officer named Pontmercy out alive.
The battle that made Georges Pontmercy a colonel and a baron, an hour before he fell.

description.text: In May 1861 the narrator, walking from Nivelles, comes to an old walled farm with a cannonball hole in its gate. It is Hougomont, and he is standing on the field of Waterloo.
At Hougomont, Napoleon's first obstacle, three thousand men died in one enclosure; its well was filled with corpses. Now a peasant will explain the battle for three francs.

Hugo argues that the rain of 17–18 June lost Napoleon the battle: the wet ground delayed his guns until half-past eleven and gave Blücher time to come. He sets out not to write military history but to judge 'like the populace'.
He lays the field out as a capital A: the two roads its legs, the sunken road from Ohain its crossbar, Wellington on the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean at its apex, Napoleon at its foot.

At four o'clock Ney's three thousand five hundred cuirassiers charge up the slope at the English squares, and the leading ranks find the hollow road of Ohain at their horses' feet. It fills with men and horses. Hugo declares that God had decided Napoleon's fall.
The 'cloud' Napoleon took for Grouchy is Bülow's Prussians, led out of the woods by a shepherd who knew the one road fit for artillery.

The Guard goes into the fight knowing it will die. The army breaks and runs, and the last square, under Cambronne, answers a call to surrender with a single obscene word. Hugo calls that word the true victory of the day.
Hugo refuses to like Waterloo. It was the monarchies of Europe defeating the Revolution, and yet even the Restoration that followed had to grant a charter.

After the last shot, marauders strip the dead by moonlight. One of them, with a sutler's cart waiting nearby, robs a buried officer in the hollow road and in doing so drags him out alive. The officer thanks his 'rescuer', who gives his name as Thénardier. His own is Pontmercy.
In Thénardier's version, told over his inn's counter at Montfermeil, he carried a wounded general out of the grapeshot. His sign shows it.

Georges Pontmercy, chief of a squadron of cuirassiers, took the standard of the Lunenburg battalion and threw it at the Emperor's feet, his face cut open. Napoleon made him colonel, baron and officer of the Legion of Honour on the spot. An hour later he fell into the ravine of Ohain.
His dying note tells Marius that a sergeant named Thénardier saved his life on that field. Marius believes it, and so the robbery becomes, for him, a debt.
At the Café Musain a passing mention of Waterloo sets off Marius's passionate defence of Napoleon before the Friends of the A.B.C.
Marius pays the debt at last: 'Waterloo protects you,' he tells Thénardier, and Thénardier corrects him that it was a general.

moments.text: The cuirassiers fell into the hollow road of Ohain.
Cambronne's last square refused to surrender.
Thénardier robbed Pontmercy and was thanked for saving him.
Pontmercy was made colonel and baron by Napoleon on the field.

tagline.text: A decrepit house on the bleak southern edge of Paris, where Valjean hides with Cosette.
The hiding-place Valjean flees at night when Javert takes a room in it.
A house now full of poor lodgers: the Jondrettes in one garret, a young man called M. Marius next door.
Where a hole in a partition lets Marius watch the Jondrettes' den.
The house where a trap is being laid for a benefactor.
The scene of the Thénardier ambush, raided by Javert.

description.text: Numbered 50–52 on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, in the waste lands near the Salpêtrière where Paris turns into nothing. It is known by the name of an old lawyer, Maître Gorbeau, said to have owned it. From the road it looks like a hovel, but it is enormous inside: a door and one big patched window on the street, a steep ladder of a staircase, and a long corridor of rooms more like stalls than chambers. Around it lie the city wall, the road to Bicêtre and the Salpêtrière, neither city nor country.

Jean Valjean carries the sleeping Cosette into a prepared attic on Christmas night 1823. In the morning she gets up expecting to work and is told to play. They live there for weeks in great quiet and happiness, he discovering love and she being loved.
The only other occupant is the old woman who keeps the house. She watches Valjean, sees his thousand-franc note, and talks about it.
A new lodger arrives and listens at Valjean's door by night. Valjean sees his back at dawn and knows him for Javert. He leaves with Cosette at nightfall.
Javert had traced 'the beggar who gives alms' here, rented a room, and listened at his door, and the old woman warned him when Valjean was about to go.

Eight or nine years later the house is full, every lodger poor. The old portress is dead and another has replaced her. The poorest household is a family of four in one garret who call themselves Jondrette; their son, the gamin Gavroche, visits every two or three months and finds nothing there for him. The neighbour across the partition is a poor young man known as M. Marius.
Marius has a fireless closet here for thirty francs a year, and pays the portress three francs a month to sweep it and bring his breakfast.
He secretly pays twenty francs of rent to save the Jondrettes from being evicted.
By the winter of 1832 almost all the lodgers have gone except Marius and the Jondrettes.

High in the thin wall between Marius's room and the Jondrettes' garret he finds a triangular hole. He climbs onto his commode and looks into a filthy den with leprous walls and obscene charcoal drawings, two pallets and a brazier.
Through the hole Marius watches the girl of the Luxembourg and M. Leblanc arrive with clothes and blankets for the family he thought he knew.

The house will be empty at six: the neighbour dines out, the portress washes dishes in town. Jondrette prepares a brazier, a chisel, ropes and a rope ladder, and four blackened men wait in an empty attic along the corridor.
So the house has held them both. The white-haired benefactor tied up in the garret is the man who once fled this house with Cosette, and Jondrette is Thénardier.
Javert comes in at the door and takes the whole gang, but the victim gets out through the window.
Gavroche kicks at the locked door the next night and is told his whole family is in prison.
Marius leaves the house the morning after the ambush, to escape being a witness, and moves in with Courfeyrac.
Marius never told Cosette about the Gorbeau drama. Now that he knows her guardian was a convict, he concludes that Valjean fled the ambush because he was a fugitive.
Thénardier's letter brings the Jondrette garret straight back to Marius by its smell and handwriting. Marius tells Thénardier he saw him in his lair on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital.

moments.text: Valjean brought Cosette here after Montfermeil.
Javert took a room; Valjean and Cosette fled.
Marius found the hole in the partition.
Jondrette named himself Thénardier in the ambushed garret.
Javert raided the garret and arrested the gang.

aliases.name: the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration

tagline.text: A lost old quarter of Paris where Valjean, hunted, runs into a blind alley.
A vast silent garden behind a high wall, and a dark building where women sing.
A convent of cloistered nuns, where old Fauchelevent is gardener.
The strictest convent in Paris, where Hugo pauses the story to study the cloister.
Valjean's refuge: he is its second gardener, Cosette a pupil.
The convent Valjean and Cosette left so that she could choose her own life.

description.text: Fleeing Javert across the Pont d'Austerlitz, Valjean takes the road to the open country and finds himself in the Petit-Picpus, an old quarter Hugo traces on a 1727 plan of Paris. He is trapped between a blind alley and a sentinel.
At the angle of the Rue Droit-Mur and the Rue Polonceau stands a sombre building whose drainpipe will not bear his weight and whose great door is only boarding over stone.
He climbs the wall with Cosette tied to a lantern rope and drops into a garden as Javert's men search the alley.
Inside: a vast, melancholy garden, façades barred and dark. A hymn of women's voices rises from the building and both of them kneel.
Through a lighted window Valjean sees a shrouded figure lying face down with arms outstretched and what looks like a rope round its neck, and flees in terror.

A man with a bell on his knee is covering melons against the frost. He is Fauchelevent, the carter Valjean saved, placed here as gardener. The house is a convent; the bell warns the nuns to keep away from the only man allowed in the garden.

Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus: a carriage gate, a stair, a grated hole, a password, and a parlour where a veiled nun may speak and never be seen. It is the convent of the Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga, of the Perpetual Adoration.

Their rule: black habits, fasts, scourging, silence, night offices, and the reparation, in which a nun lies twelve hours face down before the sacrament with a rope round her neck. That was the figure Valjean saw. Only the prioress may deal with the outside world, through the parlour.
Novices take the veil to the office of the dead. Attached to the convent is a school for well-born girls, who see even their mothers only through bars.

The enclosure holds the Great Convent, the school, and the Little Convent, a refuge for old nuns of orders destroyed by the Revolution. The church is built so that no one in the cloister can see a face from outside.

In 1819–1825 its prioress is the learned and merry Mother Innocente. The house talks by a code of bells, and the pupils see only two men besides the archbishop and the gardener: an old, ugly chaplain and a hunchbacked drawing-master.

By 1840 the school and the Little Convent were gone and the nuns had dwindled to a handful. Hugo explains that he has entered this house because it is part of Jean Valjean's story, and that he looks at it with respect but without belief.
Closing his 'Parenthesis' on convents, Hugo condemns monasticism as history but salutes the person who kneels. There must be some, he says, who pray constantly for those who never pray.
To stay, Valjean must first get out and come back in by the door. Any man found in the garden would be discovered by the pupils.

The plan works. A nun is buried in secret under the chapel altar, Valjean leaves in her official coffin and comes back by the front door as Ultime Fauchelevent, and Cosette is admitted as a charity pupil.

Years pass. Valjean gardens beside Fauchelevent, sees Cosette an hour a day, and never goes out. He compares this cloister with the galleys, is humbled by women doing penance for others' sins, and prays every evening outside the chapel window.
When Fauchelevent died, Valjean asked himself whether he had the right to keep Cosette there before she was old enough to choose. He took her out of the convent and moved to the Rue Plumet.
The nuns, never sure which Fauchelevent Cosette belonged to, give glowing references when Valjean makes her the dead gardener's orphan daughter for her marriage.

moments.text: Valjean scaled the wall with Cosette, escaping Javert.
Fauchelevent recognised Father Madeleine in the garden.
Valjean was admitted as gardener and Cosette as pupil.
Valjean and Cosette left the convent.

name: The house in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire

tagline.text: M. Gillenormand's house in the Marais, shut all day, open after dinner.
The house Marius was ordered out of.
Where Marius is carried home, apparently dead, from the barricade.
Where Marius and Cosette marry and set up house.
The house where M. Fauchelevent is received each evening in a damp room downstairs.

description.text: M. Gillenormand owns No. 6 in the Marais and lives in a vast first-floor apartment between street and garden, hung with Gobelins and Beauvais tapestries, with a little staircase from his window down into the garden.
He retired here after eighty. The door stays shut all day and opens only after dinner at five.
Besides the porter, the household is a maid called Nicolette and a valet called Basque.
In the salon Marius tells his grandfather what his father was, shouts 'Down with the Bourbons!', and is told 'Be off!'. He leaves with thirty francs.
Four years later he rings at its door to ask permission to marry, and leaves it again, insulted.
On the barricade Marius writes a note asking that his body be carried to his grandfather, M. Gillenormand, 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, in the Marais.
Deep in the sewer Valjean reads that note in Marius's pocketbook and knows where to take him.
Javert's coach stops at its knocker of goat and satyr at night. The porter, Basque, Nicolette and the aunt are woken and Marius is laid on a sofa in the antechamber; the grandfather is left asleep.
Marius lies here for months between life and death. Every day a well-dressed white-haired gentleman calls at the porter's lodge and leaves lint.
The couple are to live here. The grandfather gives up his own room, hung with buttercup satin, and turns his library into Marius's study.
The wedding party comes back here on 16 February 1833. Marius climbs in triumph the stairs he was carried up dying, and at the banquet one armchair beside the bride stays empty.
M. Fauchelevent asks to be received not upstairs but in a damp, cobwebbed ground-floor room.
Then the fire in that room is not lit, the armchairs go, and he understands he is being shown the door.
Here, in Marius's study, Thénardier comes to sell a secret and gives away the truth.

moments.text: Marius was turned out by his grandfather.
Marius was brought home from the barricade at night.
The wedding banquet was held here.
Thénardier's visit revealed who had saved Marius.

tagline.text: A little café near the Panthéon whose back room is the students' meeting place of the Friends of the A.B.C.
The noisy back room where Marius's certainties come apart.
The room where Enjolras hands out the work of the coming insurrection.

description.text: The Friends of the A.B.C. meet in two places: Corinthe, a wine-shop near the fish-market, close to the workmen, and the Café Musain in the Rue Saint-Michel near the Panthéon, close to the students. The café has since been torn down. Their assemblies are usually held in its back room.
Laigle, lounging outside its door, hails the cab carrying Marius, newly homeless, and Courfeyrac comes out of the café to take him in.
Courfeyrac introduces Marius in the back room as 'a pupil'. The free talk there unsettles everything Marius thought he had fixed; none of them says 'the Emperor'.

An evening in the back room: Grantaire drunk and declaiming, Bossuet on law, two men drafting a vaudeville, Prouvaire defending the pagan gods, and Courfeyrac throwing a copy of the Charter into the fire.
Here Marius makes his passionate defence of Napoleon, and Combeferre answers him in two words: 'To be free'.
Shaken and isolated, Marius stops going.
In April 1832 Enjolras holds a secret meeting here and sends each of his friends to sound out a group of possible fighters across Paris.

moments.text: Courfeyrac came out of the café and took Marius home with him.
Marius defended Napoleon to the A.B.C.; Combeferre answered 'To be free.'
Enjolras assigned his lieutenants.

tagline.text: A wine-shop near the Halles, the workmen's end of the Friends of the A.B.C.
Mother Hucheloup's old wine-shop in the Rue de la Chanvrerie, where the friends eat badly out of loyalty.
The wine-shop with a barricade built against its walls, now the insurgents' fortress.
The wine-shop where the last defenders died, Enjolras and Grantaire in the room upstairs.

description.text: One of the two meeting places of the Friends of the A.B.C.: a wine-shop near the fish-market, close to the workmen.
Its secret meetings are held in a restaurant wine-shop of the Rue Mondétour.

It stood for three hundred years at the corner of the Rue de la Chanvrerie, in a tangle of streets by the Halles that Hugo draws as a letter N. Once called the Pot-aux-Roses, it got its name when a painter paid for his drinking by painting a bunch of Corinth grapes on its post. It has a taproom and kitchen below, a billiard-room up a spiral stair, and a trapdoor to the cellar. Father Hucheloup, a growling former fencing-master, made famous stuffed carp. He died about 1830, the carp died with him, and his bearded widow kept the place going with two serving-maids, Matelote and Gibelotte. The cooking is now execrable, and Courfeyrac's friends keep coming 'out of pity'. Grantaire discovered it.
On the morning of 5 June Bossuet, Joly and Grantaire breakfast here and stay drinking all afternoon, until Enjolras's armed band passes the door.
In minutes the street outside is barred with paving-stones, a dray, the widow's casks and an overturned omnibus. The wine-shop is the barricade's keep.
Courfeyrac tells the widow her table is avenging the hundred-franc fine she once paid. Bullets are cast from her pewter on the hearth, and the women make lint.
The unmasked police spy is tied to a post in the taproom.
Mabeuf, who has sat silent behind its counter since the barricade went up, rises to carry the flag, and his body is brought back in.
Before the last assault its windows are walled with paving-stones and bottles of aquafortis carried upstairs. The last man to leave the taproom is to shoot Javert.
When the barricade falls Enjolras holds the door alone to let the survivors in, and they fight on from the first floor with their last cartridges and bottles.

The soldiers break into the upper room and find Enjolras alone on his feet; Grantaire wakes from his drunken sleep there to die with him. The last insurgents are hunted down in the attic and the cellar.

moments.text: Bossuet, Joly and Grantaire spent the morning of 5 June drinking here.
The barricade went up against its walls.
Enjolras and Grantaire were shot in the room upstairs.

tagline.text: The Paris garden where Marius walks alone in its quietest alleys.
Where Marius sees the same white-haired man and girl on the same bench every day.
The garden where a glance changes Marius's life.
A garden emptied of the two people Marius came for.
Where Marius fell in love with Cosette without knowing who she was.
A deserted garden where two lost little boys fish a brioche out of the swans' basin.

description.text: Marius's pleasures are long walks alone on the outer boulevards, the Champ-de-Mars and the least frequented alleys of the Luxembourg.

For a year he has noticed at the loneliest end of the walk along the Pépinière, a white-haired man of about sixty and a thin, plain girl of thirteen or fourteen, always on the same bench. They look like father and daughter. Courfeyrac nicknames them Monsieur Leblanc, for his hair, and Mademoiselle Lanoire, for her black convent-school dress.
After six months away Marius comes back to find the same man with what seems another girl: the awkward child has become a beautiful young woman.
On a luminous spring day their eyes meet.
He comes now in his new coat, marches past the bench, and sits at a distance. He begins to feel that M. Leblanc has noticed him.
He follows them home, questions their porter, and is stared at by M. Leblanc. After that they stop coming. The bench stays empty.
In the Gorbeau garret Thénardier calls M. Leblanc the man who took the Lark from Montfermeil, so the white-haired man of the bench is Jean Valjean and the girl is Cosette.
Every day Valjean takes Cosette to walk in the quietest alley of the Luxembourg.
Hugo retells the bench from Cosette's side. The glance that troubled Marius troubled her too; she steered her father's walks past his bench, and they adored each other at a distance without a word.
Valjean senses Marius and comes to detest him, changing his hour and his bench to test him. After Marius follows them to the Rue de l'Ouest, Valjean stops coming to the Luxembourg.

During the fighting of 6 June the garden is deserted. The two little Thénardier boys Gavroche once sheltered hide by the swans' hutch while a well-fed bourgeois lectures his son and throws his stale brioche to the swans. When they leave, the elder boy fishes it out and gives the bigger half to his brother.
Valjean reminds Marius where he first saw Cosette: near the Luxembourg, in her blue plush hat.

moments.text: Marius first noticed the white-haired man and the girl.
Their eyes met.
The two stopped coming.
Two hungry boys shared a brioche from the swans' basin.

name: The house in the Rue Plumet

tagline.text: A hidden house and wild garden near the Invalides, where Valjean lives with Cosette as M. Fauchelevent.
A garden where someone leaves a stone, and under it a notebook, on Cosette's bench.
The garden where Marius and Cosette meet at last.
The house a gang comes to rob, and a girl at the gate stops them.
A house shuttered and empty, where Marius calls Cosette's name in vain.

description.text: Built in the last century by a chief justice to hide a mistress: a pavilion facing a large overgrown garden, a courtyard and a low back building, and from there a walled passage that winds for a quarter of a league between gardens to a second, secret door on the Rue de Babylone. It stood empty after the Revolution until October 1829, when Jean Valjean took it as M. Fauchelevent and moved in with Cosette and a servant, Toussaint. He also keeps two shabby lodgings in the Rue de l'Ouest and the Rue de l'Homme Armé, so that he can vanish at the first alarm.

Cosette and Toussaint have the pavilion, with gilded boudoir and canopied bed. Valjean sleeps in a fireless porter's lodge at the back of the courtyard and keeps black bread for himself. No stranger enters. They come and go only by the Rue de Babylone door; the gate on the Rue Plumet stays locked.

Left alone for half a century, the garden has grown into a fragrant wilderness behind its rusty railing. Hugo makes it a meditation: nothing in nature is small, and everything is bound to everything else.
A garden made for a magistrate's gallantries now shelters innocence. Cosette grows up here, fourteen when she leaves the convent, adoring her father.
Valjean comes home from a visit to the poor with a burned arm and is nursed for a month. In the pavilion their old closeness comes back.
A lieutenant of lancers rides past the railing every day, and Cosette watches for him.
While Valjean is away, Cosette hears footsteps in the garden at night and sees a man's shadow beside her own.
She finds a stone on her bench by the railing, and under it a notebook of unsigned love thoughts.
At dusk Marius is standing behind her bench. He has been coming into her garden at night. They kiss, talk for hours, and only at the end tell each other their names.
Through May 1832 Marius slips in every evening by a loose bar in the railing, and the garden becomes theirs.

On the night of 3 June Thénardier, out of prison, comes with Claquesous, Gueulemer, Babet, Brujon and Montparnasse to rob the house: the 'affair in the Rue Plumet, a gate on a garden' passed out of La Force. Éponine is sitting by the loose bar and faces them alone, threatening to scream, and they go away.
Cosette tells Marius her father is taking her away, perhaps to England, within the week. Marius scratches his address, 16 Rue de la Verrerie, on the garden wall.
Valjean finds the address on the wall. With Thénardier prowling the quarter, he has already decided to leave.

On the evening of 5 June Marius finds the shutters closed and the garden empty. He sits on the steps and decides that, since Cosette is gone, there is nothing left but to die. A voice from the street calls him to the barricade.
They left on the evening of 4 June for the Rue de l'Homme Armé, taking only Toussaint and the little valise.
After their marriage Marius and Cosette go back to look at their garden, and lose themselves there; Valjean waits for her in vain that evening.

moments.text: Valjean moved in with Cosette as M. Fauchelevent in 1829.
Marius and Cosette met in the garden and told each other their names.
Éponine turned away the gang at the gate.
Valjean found Marius's address scratched on the wall.

tagline.text: A quiet street in the Marais where Valjean keeps a shabby bolt-hole.
Cosette's new address, in the letter that never reached Marius.
Where Valjean reads Marius's farewell to Cosette, and goes out in his uniform.
The empty flat Valjean goes back to alone after the wedding.
Where Jean Valjean died, with Cosette and Marius at his side.

description.text: One of two poor lodgings Valjean rents under another name, far from the Rue Plumet, in case he must disappear. He stays there now and then for a month or six weeks, without Toussaint, waited on by the porters.
Cosette's note, which Éponine kept, said they would be at No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé that evening, and in England in a week. Marius sends his own farewell there by Gavroche.

On the evening of 4 June Valjean moves Cosette and Toussaint here with only 'the inseparable' valise. The quiet street gives him back his calm. Then, in the mirror over the sideboard, he reads the reversed imprint of Cosette's note to Marius on her blotter.

He is sitting on his doorpost at eleven when Gavroche comes looking for No. 7, smashes the street lantern, and lets slip that he has a letter from the barricade for Mademoiselle Cosette. Valjean takes it.
Upstairs, while Cosette and Toussaint sleep, he reads 'I die', and feels a frightful joy. Then he wakes the porter, and an hour later goes out in his National Guard uniform, armed.
At dawn Cosette wakes here, knowing nothing of the fighting, sure Marius has had her letter and will come today.
At the barricade Valjean cuts Javert loose and tells him he lives as Fauchelevent at No. 7.
Javert walks him to this door after the sewer, tells him to go up, and says he will wait. When Valjean looks out of the landing window, the street is empty.
M. Gillenormand has had the address found: the girl lives at No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé.
On his wedding night Valjean walks home here alone, takes off the sling, opens the little valise, lays out the mourning clothes Cosette wore leaving Montfermeil, and weeps over them.
Every evening through the spring and summer of 1833 he walks from here towards the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, peers round the corner, and turns back, a little sooner each day.
He takes to his bed and stops eating. His portress, the only soul he sees, fetches a doctor, who says the old man is dying of having lost someone dear to him.
He puts on his old workman's clothes, lays Cosette's little dress on the bed, and lights the Bishop's candlesticks in broad daylight, as candles are lit in a room where there is a corpse.
Marius and Cosette burst in on him here. He tells Cosette her mother's name, lays his hands on their heads, and dies.

moments.text: Valjean read Cosette's note in the mirror.
Gavroche handed over Marius's letter at the door.
Javert left Valjean at his door and vanished.
Jean Valjean died here.

tagline.text: A crumbling plaster model of a Napoleonic monument on the Place de la Bastille, and Gavroche's home.

description.text: A forty-foot model in timber and plaster of a monument Napoleon planned, left to rot in a corner of the Place de la Bastille beside the boarded-up column of July: black with weather, grass between its legs, melancholy by day and formidable by night. Gavroche gets in by a ladder to a hole in its belly. Inside, among beams and plaster stalactites, with rats in the corners, he has a straw mat, a blanket and a cage of brass wire netting against the rats. Here he puts the two lost little boys to bed. Hugo says Napoleon's idea, forgotten by the great, has become a shelter for a child.
Before dawn Montparnasse's cry calls Gavroche down from it to help with a jailbreak.
The two little boys never came back to it.

moments.text: Gavroche sheltered two lost boys inside it for the night.
Montparnasse called Gavroche out of it before dawn.

name: The barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie

tagline.text: The barricade where, says a voice in the dark, Marius's friends are waiting for him.
A barricade of paving-stones, casks and an omnibus, thrown across the street in front of Corinthe.
The barricade where old Mabeuf died raising the flag.
Marius's barricade, where Éponine died in his arms.
A barricade abandoned by Paris, where thirty-seven men stay to die, Jean Valjean among them.
The barricade Gavroche died outside, singing.
Taken: Enjolras and Grantaire shot together, the last defenders killed.
Taken. Of its defenders, only Marius was carried out alive, on Jean Valjean's back.

description.text: Marius knows only that it exists: a voice calls through the trees of the Rue Plumet that his friends are waiting for him at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.
