The Rue de la Chanvrerie runs into the old maze of streets by the Halles, and the wine-shop Corinthe stands at its corner.
Enjolras's band builds it in minutes, out of torn-out bars, paving-stones, a lime-dealer's dray, Mother Hucheloup's casks and an omnibus that Bossuet stops and overturns.

Finished, it is six or seven feet high, with steps of paving-stones inside so that the defenders can mount its crest, a gap at one end, and a red flag on the upright omnibus pole. A smaller barricade in the Rue Mondétour, behind the wine-shop, makes the whole a redoubt. Courfeyrac hands out thirty cartridges to each man, three sentinels are posted, and some fifty men wait as the light goes.
Gavroche unmasks the tall recruit from the Rue des Billettes as a police spy. He is Inspector Javert, and he is tied to a post inside.
When a drunken recruit, Le Cabuc, murders the old porter of the house at the end of the barricade, Enjolras executes him on the spot: insurrection must have discipline.
Marius, coming through the dark streets, looks into it from the elbow of the Rue Mondétour and argues himself into civil war.
At ten the troops come. 'Who goes there?' 'The French Revolution!' A volley cuts down the flagstaff.
Old Mabeuf climbs the barricade with the flag, crying 'Long live the Republic!', and falls dead under the second volley.

Marius saves Gavroche and Courfeyrac with his two pistols, a young workman in velvet trousers takes the bullet aimed at him, and Marius drives off the attack by threatening to blow up a barrel of powder with a torch. He is made chief.
Jean Prouvaire, taken prisoner, is shot by the troops; they hear his last cry.
Behind the little barricade the young workman is Éponine, dying. She tells Marius she led him there so they might die together.
Through the night they rebuild and repair, lay out the dead, and talk philosophy. By dawn thirty-seven remain.
Enjolras tells them the truth: Paris is not rising and the army is coming. A man answers that they should stay and make the protest of corpses, and all acclaim him.

Fathers and breadwinners are sent away in captured uniforms. A fifth uniform is needed, and one is thrown on the pile by a man who has just come in: Jean Valjean, in National Guard dress. Marius knows him as M. Fauchelevent.
From its paving-stone steps Enjolras speaks his vision of the future, and calls the barricade the meeting place of ideas and woes, where those who die enter a tomb flooded with dawn.
The Mondétour gap is walled up; there is no way out. A cannon is brought up.
Valjean shoots down a mattress from a distant attic window and stops the breach the grapeshot is tearing.
Gavroche goes out to empty the dead Guards' cartridge boxes and sings back at every bullet until one kills him.
Valjean asks to execute the spy himself, takes Javert behind the little barricade, cuts him loose, and fires into the air.
The army throws itself at it again and again. It holds through ten assaults, like a wall of Troy. Bossuet, Feuilly, Courfeyrac and Combeferre are killed.
The centre gives way. Enjolras holds the wine-shop door; Marius falls outside with a broken collarbone and feels a hand seize him.
Enjolras and Grantaire are shot together upstairs, the last insurgents killed in the attic and cellar, and the barricade is taken.
The hand was Jean Valjean's. He carried the unconscious Marius into the angle where Éponine died, found an iron grating under the loose stones, and went down with him into the dark.
Marius, recovering, cannot fit M. Fauchelevent into his memory of the barricade, and when Fauchelevent says he does not know the Rue de la Chanvrerie, decides he dreamed it.
Knowing now that Fauchelevent was the convict Jean Valjean, Marius decides he went to the barricade to take revenge on Javert, and killed him.
Javert's own report, printed in the Moniteur, says he owed his life at the barricade to an insurgent who fired into the air instead of killing him.

moments.text: Built in minutes in front of Corinthe.
Mabeuf was shot raising the flag.
Éponine died in Marius's arms.
Jean Valjean entered in National Guard uniform.
Gavroche was killed gathering cartridges outside it.
The barricade fell; Enjolras and Grantaire were shot.

aliases.name: the intestine of the Leviathan
aliases.note: Hugo's title for the book that describes them

tagline.text: Lutetia, the city of mud beneath the city of light, which Hugo maps before following Valjean down.
The dark labyrinth through which Valjean carries the bleeding Marius.
The sewer where Valjean almost drowns in a slough of mud, holding Marius above it.
A sewer whose locked outlet is opened by Thénardier's key.

description.text: Hugo opens the book on the sewers by arguing that Paris pours twenty-five million francs a year into the river as human manure that should feed the fields. Beneath the city of light lies Lutetia, the city of mud, a colossal sponge of galleries whose offspring is the rat.
The sewer has been sepulchre and refuge for outlaws and persecuted thought through the centuries. It is the conscience of the city, the one place where nothing lies.
From 1805 to 1812 a man named Bruneseau explored it by night, through pestilence and bottomless holes, and found an orangutan's skeleton and a scrap of Marat's shroud.
By 1832 much of the old gothic sewer was still unrepaired, with floods, quicksands and typhus.

Valjean, with Marius on his shoulders, turns away from the outlets that would bring him up into the crowded centre, climbs without knowing where he is, and sees his own shadow thrown ahead of him by a lantern behind.
A police patrol searching for insurgents listens, hears nothing, and fires one shot into the dark; it strikes the arch above Valjean's head.

Thirsty, bitten by rats and failing, he reaches the Grand Sewer at about three in the afternoon and goes downstream. Under an air-hole he binds Marius's wounds with his own shirt and reads in his pocketbook where to take him.

The pavement turns to mud: a fontis, a slough left by yesterday's rain. He sinks to his calves, his waist, his armpits, holding Marius above the water, until with only his head above the surface his foot finds the far edge of the paving. He climbs out and prays.
He sees daylight ahead and runs to the outlet on the Seine, and finds it closed by a heavy grating double-locked.

A barefoot man lays a hand on his shoulder and whispers 'Half shares'. It is Thénardier, who has made the sewer his hiding-place and has a key. He takes Valjean for a murderer getting rid of a body, takes his thirty francs, tears a strip from Marius's coat, and lets him out.

A coachman's tale tells Marius that someone carried him from the Halles to the Champs-Élysées through the sewer, a league and a half, and was arrested at the outlet. Marius calls that man an archangel, and does not know who he was.
Thénardier tells Marius the sewer story to blacken Valjean: an ex-convict with a corpse on his back. The torn strip fits Marius's bloodstained coat exactly.

moments.text: Valjean carried Marius away from the outlets and into the dark.
Valjean crossed the fontis with Marius held above the mud.
Thénardier opened the outlet and tore a strip from Marius's coat.

tagline.text: Two massive silver candlesticks, among the few fine things the poor Bishop of Digne has kept.
Lit on the Bishop's table in honour of a convict guest.
The Bishop's gift to the man who robbed him, with the silver he stole.
The one thing from Digne Valjean has kept, on his mantel as M. Madeleine.
Wrapped in an old shirt and carried off when Valjean fled Montreuil-sur-Mer.
Buried for ten years with Madeleine's fortune in the forest of Montfermeil.
Lit in broad daylight in Valjean's lonely room.
Left to Cosette: silver, but to Valjean gold and diamonds. He died in their light.

description.text: The Bishop has given away nearly everything. He still owns six silver knives and forks, a soup-ladle, and two massive silver candlesticks inherited from a great-aunt. He admits it would be hard to give them up. Madame Magloire locks the silver in a cupboard by his bed each night; the key is never taken out.
When the convict Jean Valjean is let in and given a place at table, the Bishop says the lamp gives a poor light and has Madame Magloire bring the two candlesticks and light them.
At bedtime the Bishop takes one candlestick, gives the other to his guest, and lights him through his own bedroom to the alcove.
In the night Valjean takes the basket of silver from the cupboard by the sleeping Bishop's bed, and leaves the candlesticks.

Gendarmes bring Valjean back with the silver. The Bishop greets him gladly: 'But I gave you the candlesticks too, which are silver like the rest. Why did you not carry them away?' He hands them over, and tells Valjean in a low voice never to forget that he has promised to use this silver to become an honest man. 'I buy your soul; I withdraw it from black thoughts and the spirit of perdition, and I give it to God.' Valjean has no memory of promising anything.

After the theft from Little Gervais, Valjean sold the Bishop's silver but kept the candlesticks to remind himself where he started. He hid everything from the galleys and let the candlesticks be seen: they are the two silver candlesticks on M. Madeleine's mantel. On the night of his struggle over Champmathieu he burns his old convict clothes and seizes the candlesticks to melt them too, and a voice inside him cries 'Jean Valjean!'

Escaped from the town jail, he slips back into his room one last time, tears up an old shirt, and wraps the candlesticks in the strips, eating a crust of prison bread as he works. He leaves his money for the poor and goes.
With M. Madeleine's money, withdrawn from Laffitte, he buried the candlesticks in the Blaru-bottom glade of the forest of Montfermeil. They lay there ten years, until he dug them up.

On the chimneypiece of his room in the Rue de l'Homme Armé, Valjean puts two wax candles in them and lights them, though it is broad summer daylight, as candles are lit by day in a room where there is a corpse.

Dying, he leaves them to Cosette: 'They are of silver, but to me they are gold, they are diamonds; they change candles which are placed in them into wax-tapers.' He does not know whether the man who gave them to him is pleased with him on high; he has done what he could. He dies with their light on his face.

moments.text: Lit for Jean Valjean at the Bishop's table.
Given to Valjean by the Bishop, who 'bought his soul' for God.
Nearly melted down on the night of 'A Tempest in a Skull'.
Wrapped in a shirt and taken from Montreuil-sur-Mer.
Bequeathed to Cosette as Valjean died.

tagline.text: A little Savoyard's coin, which Valjean put his foot on and would not give back.
The stolen coin that glints in the ashes of Valjean's convict clothes.
Valjean's proof to the court at Arras, waiting in his fireplace.
The theft that sent Valjean back to the galleys for life.

description.text: Leaving Digne in turmoil the morning after the Bishop's gift, Valjean sits by a road while a little Savoyard chimney-sweep, Petit-Gervais, plays with his coins. One rolls to Valjean's feet and he puts his foot on it. The child begs for his forty sous, then cries, and Valjean, in a stupor, drives him off. Afterwards he sees the coin, comes to himself in horror, and runs the plain calling the boy's name, in vain. He weeps for the first time in nineteen years.

The theft from Little Gervais makes Valjean a second offender, liable to the galleys for life. When he burns his old blouse and knapsack in the fireplace, something sparkles in the ashes: the forty-sou piece.
At Arras the prosecution charges that Jean Valjean, just out of Toulon, robbed a Savoyard child on the highway, and reserves the right to try him for it once his identity is proved.
Declaring himself, Valjean tells the court: 'You will find at my house, among the ashes in the fireplace, the forty-sou piece which I stole, seven years ago, from Little Gervais.'

The portress has picked it out of the ashes and set it on his table with the iron tips of his cudgel. He leaves them there with a note: these are the forty-sou piece stolen from Little Gervais and the tips of his cudgel, which he mentioned at the Assizes.
In 1823 he is tried for the robbery of Petit-Gervais, condemned to death, and reprieved to hard labour for life.

description.text: A ship of the Mediterranean squadron that puts into Toulon in late October 1823 after heavy weather. Convicts are working aboard when a topman loses his footing and is left dangling from a yard. A white-haired life convict breaks his ankle chain with one hammer blow, climbs the rigging and saves him. Coming down, he falls between the ships and is not found. The Toulon paper reports the drowning of convict number 9,430, Jean Valjean.
He was not dead. He fell, or rather threw himself, into the sea without his irons, swam underwater to a moored boat, hid there until night, and reached the shore.

tagline.text: A magnificent two-foot doll in a Montfermeil toy stall, which Cosette worships from the street.

description.text: Opposite the Thénardiers' inn on Christmas eve, a toy stall shows on white napkins an immense doll nearly two feet high, in a pink crepe gown, with gold wheat-ears in real hair and enamel eyes, too dear for any mother in Montfermeil. Cosette, sent out for water, stops before 'the lady' and forgets her errand. She thinks one must be a queen, or at least a princess, to have such a thing.
Walking back with the stranger, she tells him Ponine and Zelma will not let her play with their dolls; all she has is a little lead sword.

Caught cradling Éponine and Azelma's discarded doll, Cosette is screamed at and weeps. The stranger goes out and comes back with the doll from the stall and sets it in front of her: 'It is for you.' She hardly dares touch it, names it Catherine, and sits on the floor before it, motionless. She goes to bed with it in her arms.
Madame Thénardier cannot bear the sight of the doll given to Cosette in front of her own daughters.
Carried into Paris on the stranger's back, Cosette falls asleep without letting go of Catherine.
In the Gorbeau attic she wakes to find Catherine at the foot of her bed, and plays all day.
Valjean spends hours watching her dress and undress her doll and listening to her prattle.
In the convent Cosette misses it but dares not say so, until one day she tells Valjean: 'Father, if I had known, I would have brought her away with me.'
Thénardier, unmasking his prisoner in the Gorbeau garret, sneers at him as 'Mister giver of dolls'.
Alone on Cosette's wedding night, Valjean lays out her childhood clothes and remembers her no taller than that, with her big doll in her arms.
Dying, he reminds her: 'And the big doll! dost thou remember? Thou didst call her Catherine. Thou regrettedest not having taken her to the convent!'
